Cell Tour 3D Lab

Every living thing is built from cells, and every cell is a tiny factory. Cut open an animal cell, a plant cell and a bacterium to find out what each part does. Then zoom from a whole person down to a single molecule to see how each level of your body is built from the one below it. Works offline in any modern browser — no internet, login or install.

🏭 The cell as a factory

DNA → ribosome → rough ER → Golgi → membrane

The nucleus holds the instructions, ribosomes build proteins, the Golgi ships them, and mitochondria supply the energy.

🔎 The big idea

structure fits function, at every level

Organism → organ system → organ → tissue → cell → organelle → molecule. Each level is made of the one below, and its shape suits its job.

All 3D cell and body models and simulations: © Digital Vector · digitalvector.com.au. Models are simplified for teaching. Shapes are tidied up and the colors are not real.

Teacher notes

Two self-contained labs in one offline HTML file. Open it in Chrome, Edge, Safari or Firefox (Chromebooks included). Nothing is uploaded and no student data is collected.

Suggested sequence (2 class periods)

  • Lab 1 (1 period): organelle structure and function in an animal cell, a plant cell and a bacterium; Find It quiz; a compare table (which cells have which structures); true relative sizes; and the path of an exported protein (nucleus → rough ER → vesicle → Golgi → membrane).
  • Lab 2 (1 period): the seven levels of organization, using nutrient absorption in the small intestine as the running example; scale and magnification calculations; six specialized cells and how structure fits function.

What the models assume

  • Cells are drawn as tidy cut-aways with false colors. Real cells are crowded and mostly colorless. Sizes quoted are typical values; real cells vary widely.
  • Lysosomes and centrioles are marked as animal-cell structures, as in most high school texts. (Plant cells use the vacuole for digestion; a few plant cells have centrioles.)
  • The surface area of the small intestine is given as about 30 m² (about 320 ft²), from recent measurements. Older textbooks give about 250 m² (“a tennis court”).
  • The transport protein at the molecule level is a simplified shape, not a real protein structure.

Standards

  • NGSS: HS-LS1-2 (develop and use a model to illustrate the hierarchical organization of interacting systems that provide specific functions within multicellular organisms); supports HS-LS1-1 and HS-LS1-4 (differentiation). Crosscutting concepts: structure and function; scale, proportion and quantity.
  • Texas TEKS (Biology, §112.42): B.5B (compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells); B.6B (cell specialization through differentiation); B.12A (interactions among body systems, including nutrient absorption).
  • Common Core: RST.9-10.4 (domain-specific words); RST.9-10.7 (translate between words, tables and visuals); HSN-Q.A.1 (use units to guide multistep problems).
  • AP Biology: Unit 2 — 2.1 Cell Structure: Subcellular Components; 2.2 Cell Structure and Function; 2.3 Cell Size.

Risk assessment

  • Screen-only activity: no chemicals or equipment. The models have no flashing content. If you pair it with real microscope work, follow your usual glass-slide and stain precautions.

Accessibility

  • Every 3D part can also be chosen from a button list, so nothing depends on clicking the 3D view. All questions and tables work with the keyboard. Right and wrong answers are marked with ✓ and ✗ as well as color.

Controls

  • Drag to rotate · scroll or pinch to zoom · right-drag or two-finger drag to pan. Gray buttons explain why they cannot be used yet when you tap them.
